title: Multi-tiering cost sensitivity & hosting intake - BridgePoint Labs
summary: Intro discovery to understand BridgePoint's cost targets and hosting constraints. Discussed per-token economics, batching and caching levers, and tradeoffs for hosted vs dedicated vs private. Agreed to run a short pilot bench and share a unit-cost worksheet and security docs.
next_steps: Redwood: send unit cost worksheet + example batching profiles (Maya) by 2026-10-22
Customer: provide 2 week typical traffic profile and sample prompts (Evan) by 2026-10-23
Schedule pilot kickoff with SE-run benchmark for 1 week (target 2026-10-27)
action_items: Maya: Prepare and send per-token unit economics spreadsheet by 2026-10-22
Liam: Share SOC2 report, network/VPC packaging notes, and benchmark runbook by 2026-10-21
Evan: Export 14-day traffic histograms and 50 sample prompts by 2026-10-23
transcript:
[00:00] Maya Patel: Hi everyone, thanks for making time. I'm Maya from Redwood, and with me is Liam O'Connor, our solutions engineer. Can you do quick intros?
[00:08] Evan Torres: Yeah, sure. Evan here, head of ML at BridgePoint. We're exploring options for inference hosting, cost sensitivity is the big driver.
[00:14] Priya Singh: Priya, CTO. We need to understand security/residency and what tradeoffs look like.
[00:18] Marcus Lee: Marcus, infra. I'll be evaluating network and integration constraints.
[00:22] Maya Patel: Great. High level, is the ask a single endpoint or multiple product tiers?
[00:28] Evan Torres: Multiple. We have a consumer-facing summarization feature that needs low latency, and an internal analytics batch job that can tolerate higher throughput and lower cost.
[00:36] Liam O'Connor: Okay so two clear profiles. Summarization = latency sensitive, likely smaller sequence lengths but high QPS. Analytics = batchy, longer sequences, tolerant to latency. That maps well to mixing hosted for the consumer-facing piece and dedicated or private for analytics if you want lower unit cost.
[00:49] Priya Singh: Can you quantify "lower unit cost"? Our finance wants clear per-token numbers and how batching, caching, quantization affect them.
[00:58] Maya Patel: Totally. For hosted Redwood API our public per-token price is a starting point, but what matters for you are effective unit costs after batching and caching. Liam, do you want to walk through an example?
[01:08] Liam O'Connor: Sure. If you send single-shot summarization requests with 128 token outputs and minimal prompt length, with hosted routing and small batch sizes, the latency SLO will push us to smaller batches — per-token compute cost will be higher. But if we route longer analytics jobs to Dedicated with continuous batching and KV cache across requests, you reduce compute per token by ~30-60% depending on model and QPS.
[01:29] Evan Torres: That 30-60% is huge. How deterministic is that? Our volume is spiky — mornings spike 4x.
[01:37] Liam O'Connor: The delta depends on three things: model type and quantization, sequence lengths, and QPS distribution. Spiky traffic reduces batching efficiency unless you use queueing strategies or burst autoscale. Dedicated gives you reserved GPUs so you can accept higher batch latencies and keep unit costs low; hosted optimizes for stability and transparent pricing but less control.
[01:55] Marcus Lee: For private hosting, we need to keep data inside our VPC. Does Redwood Private require special network setup?
[02:01] Maya Patel: Private can run in a VPC with customer-managed subnets and KMS integration. Liam can share the network diagram. There's some overhead to deploy — initial setup and sizing — but it can be worth it for data residency and lower marginal cost at scale.
[02:15] Priya Singh: On pedigree — do you have SOC2 and audit logs? Our security team will ask.
[02:19] Liam O'Connor: Yes, SOC2 Type II; we also offer audit logs and integrations with common SIEMs. I'll email the kit after the call.
[02:26] Evan Torres: Back to price math — can you walk through an example where we can hit a target of $0.00X per 1k tokens? We have a strict budget.
[02:34] Maya Patel: We can. It depends on what X is. For rough math: hosted per-token might be higher for low-latency single-shot calls. If you accept slightly higher latency or push analytics to dedicated or private with batching and cache, you can often reduce CPI by 2-3x versus naive single-shot hosted. I'll send a worksheet.
[02:52] Evan Torres: What's the effort to run an A/B bench vs your hosted endpoints vs a dedicated pool?
[02:58] Liam O'Connor: We can spin a short pilot. For hosted we can provide a controlled load test against our endpoints. For dedicated we can provision a small reserved pool (usually couple GPUs) for a week for benchmark runs — needs a PO for reserved capacity but we can do a limited eval arrangement. For private, it depends on network setup but SE will run the same bench.
[03:18] Priya Singh: Any gotchas with prompt caching? We worry about prompt variability.
[03:22] Maya Patel: Prompt variability reduces prefix cache hits. But KV cache at generation time helps for repeated conversational contexts. Batching is orthogonal — if many similar prompts arrive concurrently, batching helps; if prompts are unique, caching helps less. Liam: we also have prefix hashing heuristics we can tune.
[03:35] Liam O'Connor: Right. We can show a sample hit-rate analysis. For BridgePoint's summarization, if the prompt patterns are consistent (same template, different docs) we should see decent cache utility. For free-form user input, caching is limited.
[03:47] Marcus Lee: Network egress/ingress costs — if we go dedicated in cloud, do you bill for traffic?
[03:52] Maya Patel: Redwood doesn't add extra egress charges — you'll pay cloud egress on Private deployments if data crosses zones; for hosted our billing is per-token and includes inference networking between Redwood infra and model runtime. We'll add specifics in the worksheet.
[04:07] Evan Torres: What about model variants? If we pick a smaller quantized model for analytics, does your routing handle fallbacks to larger models for quality checks?
[04:14] Liam O'Connor: Yes, smart routing can fallback by policy. You can route by latency or cost, and have a canary on a larger model for a percentage of requests for QA. That helps measure quality vs cost tradeoffs.
[04:26] Priya Singh: SLA — for consumer-facing summarization we need 99.9 p50 p95 latency SLOs. Is that realistic on hosted?
[04:34] Maya Patel: We publish latency profiles. Hosted can hit those percentiles for short sequences with streaming. For stricter SLOs and capacity guarantees, Dedicated with reserved pools is the path — SLA-backed.
[04:44] Evan Torres: Ok. For decision timeline, we need to propose something to finance in two weeks. Would a pilot be sufficient to decide?
[04:51] Maya Patel: Yes, a one-week benchmark on production-ish traffic plus the cost worksheet should be enough to present to finance. We'll scope the pilot to include consumer flows and one analytics batch job.
[05:00] Marcus Lee: Any integration friction — SDKs, auth?
[05:03] Liam O'Connor: We have REST and SDKs (python/node), and support SSO and API keys. For Private there are edge connectors and a small agent for KMS. We'll share implementation notes.
[05:12] Priya Singh: Great. How do you surface tokenization differences? Finance gets confused when token counts vary by tokenizer.
[05:17] Maya Patel: Good point. Our worksheet will show tokenization examples using your sample prompts so the per-token math is apples-to-apples.
[05:24] Evan Torres: Sounds good. Anything else?
[05:26] Maya Patel: Quick recap: Redwood will send unit cost worksheet, batching profiles, SOC2 & network docs, and propose pilot dates. BridgePoint will send traffic histograms and sample prompts. We'll aim to kick off the benchmark week starting 2026-10-27.
[05:38] Priya Singh: Perfect. Thanks everyone.
[05:40] Evan Torres: Thanks Maya, Liam.
[05:41] Maya Patel: Thanks all. We'll follow up with the packet.
[05:45] [call end]
notes: Customer explicitly requested tokenization examples in worksheet
SE to include sample bench runbook and what telemetry Redwood will expose (latency by route, token counts, batch sizes)
